ch52.note: Kondō signs his recruiting writ with the campaign alias, adding a courtly given name, Masayoshi, to complete the disguise of a shogunal officer. The promise it carries, reward once the Tokugawa fortunes are restored, is the same dream of a Kōshū fief he has been chasing since Edo; issued over a false name to villagers who have never heard of the Shinsengumi, it measures how far the corps has drifted from the sworn brotherhood it began as.

Risei is a bookish, Chinese-derived word for a village head, grander-sounding than the everyday shōya or nanushi the narrator glosses it with. Amemiya reaches for it, along with a warlord ancestor and a claim to bear a surname, to dress a farmer’s standing in samurai dignity, exactly the pretension Kondō himself is living out on a larger scale.

ch52.anchor: This Amemiya Keijirō, at this time
ch52.note: Amemiya Keijirō (1846–1911) was a real man and became a far larger one than this scene suggests. A Kōshū headman’s son, he turned after the Restoration to business, built a steam-powered flour mill at Fukagawa around 1880, and rode a career of bold speculation, tramways, colliery, and above all railways, to a great fortune and the nickname “the railway king of Meiji.” Shiba’s aside, down to the water-pipe graft scandal that briefly jailed him and his death in the forty-fourth year of Meiji, is accurate; the swaggering youth who bolts at the first shell here is the same man.

A shaguma was a great flowing crest of dyed animal hair (yak or bear) worn over a commander’s helmet or cap in the new-government armies, a badge of rank visible across a battlefield. As the next lines set out, the color told the domain: Satsuma black, Chōshū white, Tosa red. Harada can read the enemy from the crest alone before a shot is fired.

The memory is of the aftermath of the Hamaguri Gate affair of 1864: when the Chōshū attack on the palace failed, a band of loyalists withdrew to Tennōzan, the hill above the Yamazaki defile between Kyoto and Osaka, and there the veteran ideologue Maki Izumi and sixteen companions took their own lives rather than be captured. The Shinsengumi, first up the hill, found only the dead. That Nagakura should recall it now, climbing another hill four years later against men riding the tide they once fought, is the chapter’s bitter mirror.

ch52.anchor: the first cannon-shot of the eastern campaign
ch52.note: The action here is the Battle of Katsunuma, also called the Battle of Kashio (柏尾), fought on the sixth day of the third month of Keiō 4 (29 March 1868). Itagaki’s Tosa-led vanguard of the Tōsandō column broke Kondō’s Kōyō Chinbutai in about two hours and drove it back toward Edo. Small as it was, it was the first land battle of the war east of the mountains and the stroke that finished the Shinsengumi as a fighting corps; within days it would disband, and Kondō’s road runs from here to Nagareyama and the execution ground.
